extracted.intended_audience: writers (especially literary authors, small-press contributors, and those considering publicizing award nominations)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating what a Pushcart Prize nomination means and deciding whether/how to publicize it (in bios, cover letters, social media) and understanding the nomination/selection process and its career/psychological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination eligibility and limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may nominate up to six pieces in any genre from work that appeared in their pages that year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies who can nominate (editors of small presses/journals) and the per-editor cap of six nominations; establishes the basic procedural eligibility for a Pushcart nomination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: A panel of previous Pushcart Prize winners and editors select the winners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that winners are chosen by a panel of past winners/editors rather than by public vote, indicating a curated selection process after nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize mission (focus on small presses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pushcart Prize Anthology's mission was (and is) to celebrate the best work coming out of the small, independent presses each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the award’s purpose and why it is especially esteemed within the small-press ecosystem; relevant when assessing the nomination's provenance and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination frequency vs. winner rarity
rubrics_metrics.description: With 1,800 journals nominating six writers apiece, this means at least 10,800 writers are nominated every year; the 2020 edition, for example, features the work of just 70 writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifies how common nominations are compared with the small number of winners, supporting the view that nominations are widespread while wins remain rare and therefore more selective/prestigious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception: publicizing nominations can appear uninformed
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Dear Writers who post resumes/bios with ‘Pushcart Nominated,’ Stop. You’re embarrassing the literary community. You’re embarrassing yourself.’ — criticism that a Pushcart nomination 'only looks good to people who don’t have the slightest clue how the [Pushcart] Prize works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: listing 'Pushcart Nominated' on resumes/bios may be viewed negatively by those familiar with the nomination volume; use caution when publicizing nominations to audiences that understand the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception: celebrating nominations is valid (esp. for marginalized writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue writers should absolutely celebrate their nominations; for some writers (e.g., those whose voices are suppressed in their countries), a Pushcart nomination is recognition they might never have dreamed of achieving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pro-publicizing rationale: emotional validation, visibility for marginalized voices, and the subjective value of feeling 'seen'; depending on context, celebration can be appropriate and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on mentioning nominations in cover letters/queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed guidance: some writers mention nominations in cover letters/queries if there is space or if readers may not know the Pushcart (e.g., international contexts); others say 'Unless you actually win, it’s best not to crow about it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context-dependent best practice: consider your audience and space constraints — in some markets (or when submissions ask for notable acknowledgments) a nomination may be useful to mention; in other contexts, avoid emphasizing nominations that are not wins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/creative impact of nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations can be 'a massive confidence booster' and can 'validate my career choice,' changing a writer’s relationship to their work and helping their writing 'blossom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat nomination as a personal/psychological metric: even without professional consequences, nominations can interrupt self-doubt, boost morale, and encourage continued risk-taking and development in craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial nomination as a quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors try to nominate the strongest pieces from the year, so being nominated was an honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While nominations are numerous, within the context of a given journal the nomination indicates the piece was considered one of that journal’s best that year — an editorial endorsement that can carry weight when communicating with some readers or peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination’s limited long-term career impact (vs. winning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being nominated made me feel like a real 'writer' and may have opened a few doors, but it didn't change my career; winning has a stronger effect on a writing career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets realistic expectations: nominations alone rarely transform a career, though they may provide minor opportunities or credibility; winning is more likely to have measurable career impact.
